Retelling: After Ehud came Shamgar, son of Anath. The whole account of his deliverance is a single verse: he slew six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, and he also delivered Israel. No oppression is named, no battle is described, and no years of rest are counted. A farmer's tool in an ordinary man's hand became the weapon by which God broke Philistine power over his people for a season. The verse places him after Ehud in the sequence of judges, and before Deborah and Barak, who are the next deliverers the book names.
Discussion: Shamgar's story is told in one verse, and that brevity is itself the point worth noticing: God is not limited to trained soldiers or proper weapons. An ox goad, the tool of a working man, was enough. Reflect: 1) What ordinary tool or skill in your hands might God use? 2) Why do you think Scripture preserves a one-verse deliverance at all? 3) How do you value faithful people whose whole story is never told?
Significance: Shamgar's single-verse deliverance shows God using an unlikely man and an ordinary tool to save Israel. Doubt: the account is one verse with no oppression, battle, or period of rest named, so its place and scale in the judges sequence cannot be fixed from the text alone.
